energy sources that will run out, such as coal, oil and gas
energy sources that are naturally replenished, such as wind and solar
fuel formed from ancient organisms, such as coal, oil and gas
the total greenhouse gases produced by a person, product or activity

starter: Bismillah. Name three fossil fuels.
What is the energy mix?
Name two renewable sources.

teach.heading: Global distribution
bullets: China and the USA are the biggest total consumers.
Per person, HICs and oil-rich states use far more than LICs.
About 80% of world energy is still from fossil fuels (approx.).

head: Pattern
Detail (approx.)
rows: Oil, coal and gas still about 80%

teach.note: Teacher to verify with the Energy Institute and IEA. Show a map of energy use per person: Canada, USA and Gulf states high; Sub-Saharan Africa low; about 750 million people lack electricity (IEA, approx. 2022). Distinguish total and per capita. Ask pupils to explain why a populous NEE consumes a lot in total but little per person.

teach.heading: Why consumption is rising
cycle: Demand for electricity and fuel rises
Need for new sources or efficiency
teach.note: Make a causal chain with three drivers: population, industrialisation of NEEs and rising wealth (more cars, appliances, air conditioning). Ask: how can efficiency offset growth? Check.

teach.heading: Supply factors

head: Factor
Example
rows: Oil concentrated in the Middle East
Offshore wind and nuclear are expensive to build
Fracking opened new gas supply in the USA
2022 gas crisis after the war in Ukraine

teach.note: Link geography (location of reserves, e.g. oil in the Middle East, coal in China), cost (extraction and building new plants), technology (fracking, offshore wind) and politics (OPEC, wars). Example: Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 reduced gas supplies to Europe and raised prices, leading to the UK Energy Price Guarantee (approx.). Ask pupils to classify each factor.

teach.heading: Impacts of energy insecurity

check.q: Which is an impact of energy insecurity on an economy?
options: Higher costs for businesses and households
check.why: Insecurity raises prices and costs, reducing output and household budgets. The other options describe secure supply.

teach.note: Sensitive areas: drilling in the Arctic or rainforest risks spills (the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill released about 4 million barrels of oil; approx.). Economies: rising bills push families into fuel poverty and reduce industrial output. Conflict: competition for oil and gas. Pupils should give specific examples. Use the check.

teach.heading: Comparing energy sources

head: Source
Type
Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Flexible fuel; gas cleaner than coal
Dams flood land and displace people

teach.note: Ask pupils to use the table to judge each source on cost, reliability and environmental impact. Nuclear low-carbon but costly with waste storage issues. Wind and solar are intermittent. Hydro is reliable but dams alter ecosystems. Misconception: renewables have no impact: they affect wildlife and land.

practice: Describe the global pattern of energy consumption. (2 marks)
Explain two reasons why global energy demand is increasing. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Explain how politics can affect energy supply. (3 marks)
Extend: Compare one renewable and one non-renewable energy source. (4 marks)
Stretch: Assess the impacts of energy insecurity. (6 marks)
exit: Give one advantage of nuclear power.
lessons.homework: Create a table of three energy sources with one advantage and one disadvantage each.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-filled energy table. EAL: key terms with images. Stretch: link energy insecurity to a recent news event.

lessons.unit: Unit 4: Energy option (AQA 3.2.3.4; option, one of food, water or energy)
lessons.title: OPTION: Energy. Fossil fuel extraction (Alberta), sustainable options and a local renewable scheme
lessons.bigQuestion: Can we meet energy needs without harming people or the planet?
objectives: Describe and evaluate the extraction of a fossil fuel: the Alberta oil sands
Explain sustainable options: conservation, design, demand reduction and cleaner fossil fuels
Describe a local renewable scheme in an LIC/NEE
successCriteria: All: describe the Alberta oil sands and one advantage and disadvantage
Most: explain sustainable energy options
Some: evaluate a local renewable scheme
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: fuels and carbon; Design Technology: efficient buildings
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship of the Earth (khalifah) and avoiding waste (Qur'an 7:31)

keywords.def: sand or clay containing thick oil called bitumen, which must be separated before use
capturing carbon dioxide from power plants and storing it underground
using less energy through efficiency and behaviour
a small hydroelectric scheme generating power for a village
building and product design that uses less energy and resources

starter: Bismillah. Name two impacts of energy insecurity.
Define non-renewable.
Why is renewable energy not always fully sustainable?

teach.heading: Alberta oil sands
bullets: Northern Alberta, Canada, around Fort McMurray.
Canada has the world's third-largest proven oil reserves, mostly oil sands (approx.).
Production around 3 to 3.5 million barrels a day (approx.).

left.title: Advantages
points: Jobs in Fort McMurray and across Canada

right.title: Disadvantages
points: Boreal forest cleared and tailings ponds
Risks to Indigenous communities and wildlife

teach.note: Teacher to verify with the Alberta Energy Regulator and Natural Resources Canada. Methods: open-pit mining and in situ steam drilling (SAGD). Ask pupils to describe the scale of change in the boreal forest. Mention Indigenous communities such as Fort Chipewyan living downstream; concerns about water and health continue.

teach.heading: Model: weigh up an example

model.problem: Evaluate the extraction of a fossil fuel you have studied. (6 marks)
steps: Economic: the Alberta oil sands support thousands of jobs and large export income.
Social: Fort McMurray grew rapidly, but the 2016 wildfire forced about 88,000 people to leave (approx.).
Environmental: forest loss, tailings ponds and high carbon emissions per barrel.
Counter: technology such as carbon capture and land reclamation can reduce impacts.
Judgement: economic benefits are large but environmental costs are serious, so the case for extraction depends on stricter controls.
model.answer: A balanced judgement with detail and conclusion.

teach.note: Show how to give a balanced paragraph with place detail.

teach.heading: Sustainable energy options
teach.note: Use the table to link each option to action at home, school and government level. Examples: UK building regulations, LED bulbs, insulation, smart meters. Carbon capture: Boundary Dam in Saskatchewan (2014) was an early coal power station fitted with CCS (verify performance). Ask: which option is cheapest per unit saved? (Usually conservation.) Link to Islam: avoid israf (waste), Qur'an 7:31.

teach.heading: Local renewable scheme: micro-hydro in Nepal
cycle: Falls through a pipe to a turbine
Village gets electricity for lights and mills
Schools, health posts and small businesses benefit
teach.note: Use a small village scheme to show appropriate technology: a stream is diverted through a pipe to a turbine producing electricity for lights, phone charging, mills and small businesses. Many hundreds to thousands of micro-hydro plants exist in Nepal (approx.), supported by the government's Alternative Energy Promotion Centre and NGOs such as Practical Action. Teacher to choose and verify a named village scheme. Ask: how does electricity change quality of life?

teach.heading: Check understanding

check.q: Which is an example of demand reduction?
options: Building a new coal power station
Insulating a home to cut heating needs
check.why: Insulation reduces the amount of energy needed. The others increase supply, not reduce demand.

teach.note: Answer B. Ask why C is wrong (it does not reduce demand).

practice: Describe two methods of extracting oil from the Alberta oil sands. (2 marks)
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of the oil sands. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Explain two ways energy use can be reduced in homes. (4 marks)
Extend: Explain how a micro-hydro scheme improves quality of life in a village. (4 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate how sustainable a local renewable scheme in an LIC or NEE is. (6 marks)
lessons.homework: Make an energy-saving plan for your household with five actions and estimated results.
lessons.send: SEND: scaffolded comparison grid. EAL: images for terms. Stretch: calculate cost savings from LED bulbs.

lessons.unit: Unit 5: Issue evaluation (AQA 3.3.1)
lessons.title: Issue evaluation: working with a pre-release booklet and making a justified decision
lessons.bigQuestion: How do geographers weigh evidence from many sources to reach a decision?
objectives: Explain the structure of the issue evaluation paper and the pre-release booklet
Interpret mixed sources, linking physical and human geography at several scales
Weigh stakeholders' views and make and justify a decision
successCriteria: All: annotate a source and state a stakeholder's view
Most: compare options using evidence
Some: write a justified, balanced decision with a final recommendation
lessons.crossCurricular: English: argument writing; Citizenship: decision-making and democracy
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness, consultation (shura) and justice for those affected

keywords.def: a person or group with an interest in a decision
the resource booklet on a geographical issue issued before the exam
judge strengths and weaknesses and reach a conclusion
drawing together knowledge from different topics
give reasons or evidence in support of a decision

starter: Bismillah. Define stakeholder.
Name two sources of evidence a geographer might use.
What does 'evaluate' mean?

teach.heading: What the paper asks
bullets: Paper 3, Section A: issue evaluation (37 marks).
Pre-release booklet issued 12 weeks before the exam.
Sources include maps, graphs, photographs, satellite images and statements.
A clean booklet is given in the exam.

head: Feature
Detail
rows: Physical and human links at several scales
Extended evaluative answer with a decision

teach.note: Check dates and format with the latest AQA paper and arrangements; the pack records these from the specification summaries. The issue draws on content from 3.1 and 3.2, such as an issue about flood management, resources or urban change. Emphasise that no new content is needed: pupils apply what they know to the booklet.

teach.heading: Preparing the booklet
teach.note: Teach the method: read the sources once for the story; then annotate for evidence for and against; build a stakeholder table; relate each option to cost, benefit, who and where. Pupils should use own knowledge from the course, such as flood management or regeneration. Ask: which stakeholder is hardest to satisfy?

teach.heading: Practice issue: Marlow Bay (fictional)

quote.text: My family has lived here for 40 years. A sea wall protects our homes, and the town's shops depend on tourists.
quote.source: Invented statement: a Marlow Bay resident (practice resource)

teach.note: The scenario is invented for practice. Marlow Bay is a fictional coastal town with 8,000 residents; options are (A) a hard sea wall costing 20 million pounds, (B) managed retreat with relocation costing 8 million pounds, (C) a do-nothing option. Use the quotes as fictional stakeholder statements. Ask pupils to rank each option against cost, protection and fairness.

teach.heading: Weighing the options

left.title: Option A: sea wall
points: Needs maintenance and may cause erosion elsewhere

teach.note: Ask pupils to complete the compare as a class on the board, adding at least one data point from the (fictional) booklet each. Remind them that cost-benefit and fairness differ: who gains and who loses?

teach.heading: Check understanding

check.q: What is the best way to end an evaluation answer?
options: A clear judgement supported by evidence and a reason for rejecting the alternative
A personal story with no evidence
check.why: A decision must be justified using evidence and show why other options were less suitable. Lists and repetition earn little credit.

teach.note: Answer B. Pupils should note that a balanced answer includes counter-arguments.

teach.heading: Model: a decision paragraph

model.problem: Using the booklet and your own knowledge, decide which option is best for Marlow Bay and justify your choice. (9 marks)
steps: State the decision: managed retreat (option B) is best overall.
Evidence: cost is 8 million compared with 20 million for the wall (fictional data).
Link to knowledge: hard engineering can increase erosion elsewhere and needs maintenance.
Stakeholders: residents lose homes, but compensation and relocation reduce harm.
Counter: the sea wall protects the town in the short term, but may not be sustainable as sea level rises.
Conclusion: B is more sustainable and affordable, provided fair compensation is given.
model.answer: A justified decision with evidence, counter-argument and conclusion.

teach.note: Model using the starter 'On balance'. Pupils write a similar paragraph in their own words.

practice: Annotate the resident statement: identify two pieces of evidence and one value judgement. (3 marks)
Suggest why different stakeholders reach different decisions. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Compare options A and B using data from the booklet. (4 marks)
Extend: Explain how one stakeholder's view could change if new evidence was given. (3 marks)
Stretch: Make and justify a decision for Marlow Bay. (9 marks, plus SPaG)
exit: State three features of the issue evaluation paper.
lessons.homework: Choose one contemporary geographical issue from the news and build a stakeholder table with three stakeholders and their views.
lessons.send: SEND: stakeholder grid and sentence starters. EAL: glossary for evaluation terms. Stretch: write for two different stakeholder audiences. Teacher to adapt to the actual pre-release booklet when issued (12 weeks before the exam); the Marlow Bay scenario is invented.
